crop_profile.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a globally important annual cereal grown on loamy to clay soils with pH 6.0-7.5. Optimal temperatures are 10-25 °C, rainfall 300-900 mm/year, and sunlight 6-10 h/day. It requires medium water and nitrogen, with critical moisture needs during flowering. Major producers include China, India, Russia, the United States, and France. Typical yields are 3 t/ha, reaching up to 7 t/ha under optimal management. Key diseases are Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and leaf rust; main pests include aphids, Hessian fly, and wheat midge. Integrated pest management, split nitrogen fertilization, and timely harvest ensure high quality grain.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply nitrogen fertilizer to address low soil nitrogen levels
recommendation.justification: Soil analysis shows nitrogen is low, which is below wheat's preferred medium requirement. All other agronomic factors (temperature, humidity, soil pH, texture, organic carbon) are optimal, and no weather risks are present. Prompt nitrogen supplementation will restore nutrient balance, support vigorous vegetative growth, and protect the expected high yield.
actions: Confirm the current soil nitrogen level with a rapid field test or recent lab report.

Select a nitrogen source appropriate for the farm (e.g., urea 46% N or ammonium nitrate) and apply at the recommended rate of ~120 kg N ha⁻¹, split into two applications: half now (within 3 days) and the remainder at the onset of the flowering stage.
Incorporate the fertilizer into the top 10 cm of soil and irrigate lightly (surface or sprinkler) to activate the nitrogen and avoid volatilization.
Record the product type, application rate, date, and weather conditions in the farm log.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Restored nitrogen availability will promote healthy leaf development, increase grain number per spike, and raise overall wheat yield, resulting in moderate profitability improvement under the already favorable environmental and market conditions.
monitoring_plan: Week 1–2 after application: Use a chlorophyll meter or visual scouting to assess leaf greenness and detect any nitrogen deficiency symptoms.
Bi‑weekly: Review NDVI from satellite imagery (target ≥0.65) to verify vegetation health remains excellent.
At flowering: Conduct a second nitrogen split‑application if leaf greenness or NDVI indicates a decline.
Post‑harvest: Perform a soil nitrogen test to evaluate residual levels and plan the next season’s fertilization schedule.

crop_profile.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a globally important annual cereal grown on loamy to clay soils with pH 6.0-7.5. Optimal temperatures are 10-25 °C, rainfall 300-900 mm/year, and sunlight 6-10 h/day. It requires medium water and nitrogen, with critical moisture needs during flowering. Major producers include China, India, Russia, the United States, and France. Typical yields are 3 t/ha, reaching up to 7 t/ha under optimal management. Key diseases are Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and leaf rust; main pests include aphids, Hessian fly, and wheat midge. Integrated pest management, split nitrogen fertilization, and timely harvest ensure high quality grain.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply nitrogen fertilizer to address low soil nitrogen levels
recommendation.justification: Soil analysis shows nitrogen is low, which is below wheat's preferred medium requirement. All other agronomic factors (temperature, humidity, soil pH, texture, organic carbon) are optimal, and no weather risks are present. Prompt nitrogen supplementation will restore nutrient balance, support vigorous vegetative growth, and protect the expected high yield.
actions: Confirm the current soil nitrogen level with a rapid field test or recent lab report.

Select a nitrogen source appropriate for the farm (e.g., urea 46% N or ammonium nitrate) and apply at the recommended rate of ~120 kg N ha⁻¹, split into two applications: half now (within 3 days) and the remainder at the onset of the flowering stage.
Incorporate the fertilizer into the top 10 cm of soil and irrigate lightly (surface or sprinkler) to activate the nitrogen and avoid volatilization.
Record the product type, application rate, date, and weather conditions in the farm log.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Restored nitrogen availability will promote healthy leaf development, increase grain number per spike, and raise overall wheat yield, resulting in moderate profitability improvement under the already favorable environmental and market conditions.
monitoring_plan: Week 1–2 after application: Use a chlorophyll meter or visual scouting to assess leaf greenness and detect any nitrogen deficiency symptoms.
Bi‑weekly: Review NDVI from satellite imagery (target ≥0.65) to verify vegetation health remains excellent.
At flowering: Conduct a second nitrogen split‑application if leaf greenness or NDVI indicates a decline.
Post‑harvest: Perform a soil nitrogen test to evaluate residual levels and plan the next season’s fertilization schedule.

steps.finding: Apply nitrogen fertilizer to address low soil nitrogen levels
actions: Confirm the current soil nitrogen level with a rapid field test or recent lab report.

Select a nitrogen source appropriate for the farm (e.g., urea 46% N or ammonium nitrate) and apply at the recommended rate of ~120 kg N ha⁻¹, split into two applications: half now (within 3 days) and the remainder at the onset of the flowering stage.
Incorporate the fertilizer into the top 10 cm of soil and irrigate lightly (surface or sprinkler) to activate the nitrogen and avoid volatilization.
Record the product type, application rate, date, and weather conditions in the farm log.
steps.justification: Soil analysis shows nitrogen is low, which is below wheat's preferred medium requirement. All other agronomic factors (temperature, humidity, soil pH, texture, organic carbon) are optimal, and no weather risks are present. Prompt nitrogen supplementation will restore nutrient balance, support vigorous vegetative growth, and protect the expected high yield.
